snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word darash ('to seek') is the programmatic verb of Chronicles' theology. When Jehoshaphat sends teachers throughout Judah with 'the book of the law,' foreign nations voluntarily submit tribute—showing that seeking God through His word produces both spiritual transformation and geopolitical security.

Asa's covenant renewal in 2 Chronicles 15 perfectly mirrors temple covenant-making: the people gather, make binding oaths audibly before witnesses, sacrifice their substance, and experience joy and rest. This same pattern appears in Latter-day Saint temple endowment—suggesting the ancient and modern ceremonies share deep structural parallels.

When Asa faces the Ethiopian invasion with a vastly superior force, he prays: 'It is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power.' Later, when facing a smaller threat, he hires a foreign king instead of praying—and loses God's favor. The shift from radical trust to calculated politics costs him his spiritual anchor.

Hanani the seer delivers one of Scripture's most stunning statements: 'The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.' God actively searches for hearts fully committed—a vision of divine attention that undergirds all temple theology about being known by God.

Jehoshaphat removes competing worship sites (high places and Asherah poles) to enforce the theological centrality of Jerusalem's temple—the one legitimate place of sacrifice. This pattern of centralization appears in every righteous king from Asa to Hezekiah, showing that covenant faithfulness requires eliminating religious competition.

After thirty-nine years of faithful rule, Asa develops a severe foot disease and dies—yet the narrative doesn't attribute this to divine punishment but to his refusal to 'seek the LORD' in his affliction (relying instead on physicians). The story suggests that physical suffering becomes redemptive only when it drives us back to covenant seeking.
